result:
There is a particular quality to the light before sunrise, when the sky has decided to brighten but has not yet committed. A blue so quiet it almost sounds like the inside of a held breath. The world below has shed its colors. Trees are merely shapes. Roads are merely lines. Everything is reduced to its skeleton, and somehow this is when the landscape looks most honest.

I prefer this hour to full daylight. In daylight, everything announces itself. The flowers compete. The birds argue. The world is a crowded room where everyone talks at once. But in that pre-dawn blue, there is a truce. The world has not yet performed for you. It is still private.

What strikes me, after years, is how little this hour has changed. I remember watching it from a kitchen window in a house where I was nine. My grandmother's radio hummed in the next room. The floor tiles were cool. The sky outside was that same uncommitted blue, and I did not know the name for it, and I did not need to.

Now I stand at a different window in a different city. The light is the same blue. The truce holds. The world is still private, still not yet itself. For eleven minutes I am allowed to watch it become.

Then the sun crests the line, and colors rush back like a tide, and the day begins its loud work.

But the blue was real. I saw it. That is enough.

"There is a particular quality to the light before sunrise, in the hour when the sky has decided to brighten but has not yet committed. It is a blue so quiet it almost sounds like the inside of a held breath. The world below has shed its colors. Trees are merely shapes. Roads are merely lines. Everything is reduced to its skeleton, and somehow this is when the landscape looks most honest.

I think I prefer this hour to full daylight. In daylight, everything announces itself. The flowers compete. The birds argue. The world is a crowded room where everyone is talking at once. But in that pre-dawn blue, there is a kind of truce. The world has not yet performed for you. It is still private.

What strikes me, after years, is how little this hour has changed. I remember watching it from a window above a kitchen in a house where I was nine. My grandmother's radio would hum in the next room, playing something I can no longer name. The floor tiles were cool under my feet. The sky outside was that same uncommitted blue, and I did not know the name for it, and I did not need to.

Now I stand at a different window in a different city. The light is the same blue. The truce holds. The world is still private, still not yet itself, and for eleven minutes or so, I am allowed to watch it become.

Then the sun crests the line, and the colors rush back in like a tide, and the room fills with arguments and announcements, and the day begins its long loud work.

But the blue was real. I saw it. That is enough."
